title: Simone
full_review:
A down-on-his-luck director creates the perfect actress out of digital pixels in the likable drama "Simone" (New Line).

Al Pacino plays Viktor Taransky, a struggling director whose bratty star Nicola (played convincingly by Winona Ryder) bails on his latest movie citing "creative differences." Taransky uses the opportunity to rant and rave about egotistical, pampered Hollywood starlets to the studio boss and his ex-wife Elaine (Catherine Keener).

Nicola insists on no red Mike & Ikes in her candy jar. Her nanny must fly with her in first class. "She doesn't have kids," growls Taransky. And herein lies the strength of the script. It happily mocks actors and their peculiar "requests," hinting that maybe Tinseltown would be better off with "synthespians" -- computer-generated actors who don't talk back.

Fired from the studio, Taransky is about as low as he can go when he inherits a computer program that produces a simulated beauty named Simone, the name being a shortened moniker for Simulation One. A computer-generated actress, she looks like a cross between Cameron Diaz and Rebecca Romijn-Stamos (who has a bit part as Simone's movie stand-in). Her voice can be manipulated to sound like Lauren Bacall or to imitate Audrey Hepburn. But best of all, she does exactly what Taransky wants her to do, with no questions, hassles or outrageous "needs," to play the role.

Tired of actors more interested in feeding their egos than concentrating on the art, Taransky sets out to use Simone to teach Hollywood a lesson. He "inserts" her into his film as the lead, and Simone becomes a huge, and instant, success. The masses and the media become infatuated with her, and their obsession is fueled by the fact that Simone is never seen in public. She's a recluse. Worked up into a frenzy, the public only wants more of her. As her popularity skyrockets, Taransky's digital protege overshadows him. However, afraid that he will be seen as a fraud and his career ruined, Taransky is conflicted as to whether he should admit the truth behind Simone's digital allure.

Writer-director Andrew Niccol plays with the themes of identity, reality and media fascination in a film that is spiked with dry wit. The film takes some deliciously dark and comical turns, but then loses its way, always returning to one joke. Spoiled by outlandish circumstances, "Simone" is drawn from the conceit that Hollywood and the public are sure to react with fervor over a beautiful but reclusive actress with so-so talent.

Granted, both the movie world and its fans have been known to flip head-over-heels for the flavor of the month, but this vanity is dragged out a little too much. And Niccol ends on a down beat with too tidy a wrap-up for the narrative without properly probing the questions raised about whether the connections made by human beings can be replaced or duplicated by a digital creation.

Pacino is appealing as Taransky, the film's force and guide. But as Taransky goes through his rollercoaster ride of highs and lows, Pacino doesn't dig deep, keeping emotions at an interesting but pretty much superficial level. Keener, as Taransky's ex-wife, is a bit pedantic. Her whining character doesn't quite connect with the audience. However, Evan Rachel Wood, as their teen-age daughter, shines as the steady and reliable child who, without being precocious, understands more than her parents do.

The burning question is who is Simone really? In the press notes she is listed as "Simone -- as herself." But it's been revealed that Simone is played by little-known-model-turned-actress Rachel Roberts. Part pixels, part flesh and blood, Simone remains remote, however, which may have been purposeful. Yet the viewer, too, yearns to be swept up in the enthusiasm over her, but is not given the chance.

Due to brief sexual suggestiveness and fleeting crass language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
